title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated licence plate recognition system, and it happened at the point where a camera alert turns into a police stop. The camera compared only the letters and numbers on a plate, so a KU Alumni plate reading 7007 matched a stolen vehicle record for a temporary Kansas tag reading the same. The system was being used in conditions it was not built for, because Kansas issues more than 100 plate designs and about half are specialty plates, which allows the same number to appear on more than one vehicle. A separate error compounded it: the wrong plate type had been entered into the system, which is what Colwich Police discovered after making the stop.

Catching this would have required the match to include the plate's background or design, not just its characters. Wichita police have discussed training Flock to recognise plate backgrounds, and the state is moving from six digit to seven digit numbers that are not duplicated. Neither change was in place when the Spurlocks were stopped, and the second stop in Catoosa, Oklahoma, shows the same alert can travel to another department and escalate before anyone checks the plate type.

What is not established is how the wrong plate type came to be entered, or whether any agency has accepted fault. The account rests on a single outlet's investigation, and a report of a mistake is not a finding of intent.

summary:
Matthew and Leah Spurlock were pulled over in Kansas after a Flock camera flagged their minivan as possibly stolen. Their KU Alumni plate had the number 7007, and a stolen GMC pickup had a temporary Kansas tag with the same number but a different background. Colwich Police stopped them, then learned the wrong plate type had been entered into the system. About a month later, Catoosa, Oklahoma, police stopped them again after another Flock alert, drawing guns and handcuffing Matthew before the mistake was sorted out.

Wichita police Capt. Casey Slaughter said Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate designs. Kansas has more than 100 plate designs, about half specialty, so numbers can be duplicated. The state is moving from six digit to seven digit numbers that are not duplicated. Wichita police have discussed training Flock to recognize plate backgrounds. The Spurlocks are no longer worried because the stolen vehicle entry has expired, and they hope to keep their 14 year old plate.
